readerTitle: Fourteen months in, the cleaning business isn't dying or growing. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (가정 청소 서비스 → 청소업체용 일정 관리 소프트웨어) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 계속할지, 피벗할지, 접을지는 결과를 보기 전에 정한 기준과 기한으로 판단한다. 지금까지 쓴 돈이 아니라 앞으로의 증거가 결정을 정한다.
misconception: 조금만 더 버티면 결국 나아진다. 결정을 미루는 것이 가장 안전하다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. 'Pivot or persevere' 회의 개념
모든 인물과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 청소 사업: 고객 60명 × 월 $150 = 월 $9,000. 신규 월 8명, 해지 월 8명이므로 순증 0명입니다.
90일 테스트: 해지 목표 월 4명, 실제 월 6명. 신규 8명 − 해지 6명 = 순증 월 2명입니다. 목표에 못 미쳤다고 카드에 적었습니다.
소프트웨어 테스트: 기준은 60일 안에 유료 업체 5곳. 결과는 8곳 × 월 $60 = 월 $480이고 대기 12곳, 해지 0곳입니다. 브레이크다운 카드의 숫자가 본문과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
고객 명단 양도나 직원 해고 절차는 나라마다 법이 다릅니다. 카드에는 법률 조언 없이 일반적인 원칙만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Fourteen months in, the business isn't dying or growing.
body: Maya runs a home-cleaning company. She has 60 regular customers, two crews and a calendar that never empties.
Revenue has sat at $9,000 a month for half a year. She works 55 hours a week. Nothing is broken. Nothing is moving either.
For the next few cards, you are Maya. You will make three calls in a row.

image.label: A cleaning van parked beside a flat line chart
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 가정집 앞에 청소 서비스 밴이 서 있고, 밴 옆면에 평평하게 이어지는 매출 선 그래프가 그려져 있음. 운전석의 창업자는 지쳤지만 생각에 잠긴 표정. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The bucket fills as fast as it leaks.
body: Each month about 8 new customers sign up and about 8 cancel. You have savings to cover roughly a year of slow months.

options.text: Double the ad budget to outrun the cancellations
options.feedback: More customers come in, but they leave at the same rate. You pay more to stand still and learn nothing new.

options.text: Call customers who cancelled and fix their top complaint
options.feedback: Good learning. But with no target and no date, a small improvement can keep you hoping for years.

options.text: Run a 90-day test: one change, one target number, a decision date in the calendar
options.feedback: You still fix the problem, but you also decide now what result would count as success. In 90 days, the decision will be clear.

cards.title: The test missed. Something else showed up.
body: Say you chose C. Cancellations came from missed and late visits, so you set a target: cut cancellations from 8 to 4 a month. To get there, you built a simple scheduling and routing tool with a freelancer.
After 90 days, cancellations fell to 6. That missed the bar.
But three owners of other cleaning companies saw the tool and asked to use it. Two paid upfront. People didn't just praise the tool. They paid for it.

cards.title: Other cleaning companies want your tool.
body: Your own business has stalled. A side project is pulling customers toward it. You've never sold software.

options.text: Close the cleaning business now and go all in on the software
options.feedback: Two payments is a signal, not proof. You'd give up your only steady income before you know whether more buyers exist.

options.text: Ignore it. It's a distraction from the real business
options.feedback: You protect your focus, but you walk away from the only strong signal in 14 months.

options.text: Test it: get 5 paying companies in 60 days while cleaning pays the bills
options.feedback: This is a pivot to a new customer, done as an experiment. The cleaning income funds the test, and the bar is set before you see the results.

cards.title: Two businesses, side by side.
body: Say you chose C. The software brings in less money. But the cleaning business has been flat for months, and every software customer is still paying and wants more.

breakdown.label: Cleaning revenue a month
breakdown.detail: Flat. Growing by about 2 customers a month

breakdown.label: Companies on the waitlist
breakdown.detail: Asked for a demo without any ads

cards.softwareNote: In software, look at retention more than revenue at this stage. Eight companies who use the tool daily and don't cancel tell you more than $480 does.

cards.title: You can't run both well.
body: The software needs your full attention. The cleaning business still has 60 customers and four staff who rely on it.

options.text: Keep both going and split your week
options.feedback: Both get half your attention. You risk two stalled businesses instead of one.

options.text: Stop cleaning at month's end and refund prepaid visits
options.feedback: Clean and honest, but customers and staff have no time to find alternatives, and you get nothing for the customer base you built.

options.text: Wind down over six weeks: hand customers to a trusted local rival, give staff notice and introductions
options.feedback: Customers keep their cleaning, staff land jobs, and you may earn some cash. Your reputation follows you into the next business.

cards.title: Decide the bar before you see the result.
body: Each call followed the same pattern: a clear test, a target set in advance and a fixed decision date. That turns a feeling into a decision.
Without a bar, two traps appear. You keep going because of what you've already spent. Or a business that barely survives runs for years and never really lives.
Keep going, change direction and shut down are all fair outcomes. Never deciding is the real failure.

image.label: A fork in the road with three signposts and a calendar
image.brief: 갈림길 인포그래픽. 세 갈래 길에 "Persevere", "Pivot", "Shut down" 표지판. 갈림길 앞에 날짜에 동그라미를 친 달력과 목표 숫자가 적힌 메모지가 놓여 있음.

cards.title: A bar can be set wrong.
body: Eight customers is a small sample. Early buyers are often friends of friends or unusually keen. The software could still stall at 30 companies.
Some businesses also take longer to show results, like seasonal trades or products with long sales cycles. A 90-day test would judge them too early.
So set the bar from what you'd need to believe, not from what feels comfortable. When a result lands close to the line, run one more test instead of guessing.

cards.title: Set the test, the bar and the date. Then let the evidence decide.
body: Each of your three calls used an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1:** a test with a deadline is how you avoid running a business that barely survives for years (*When to pivot*, *Zombie companies*)
**Decision 2:** same tool, new customer, tested on the side (*Types of pivots*)
**Decision 3:** closing in a way that protects customers, staff and your reputation (*Shutting down well*)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down one result you'd need to see in 90 days to keep going. Then put the decision date in your calendar.
